title: Financial Dependence and Growth
research_question: Does financial development causally facilitate economic growth, and specifically does it do so by reducing the cost of external finance such that industries with greater needs for outside funding grow disproportionately faster where financial markets and institutions are more developed?
data_description: The unit of observation is an industry-country pair, covering manufacturing industries (ISIC codes within U.S. SIC 2000-3999) across 43 countries over 1980-1990. Industry-level value added, gross fixed capital formation, and number of firms come from the United Nations General Industrial Statistics. Country-level financial variables include stock market capitalization to GDP (from the IFC Emerging Stock Markets Factbook) and domestic credit to GDP and its allocation to private vs. public sectors (from IMF International Financial Statistics). Macroeconomic controls (GDP, producer price index, industrial production, exchange rates) are from IFS; investment share of GDP and average years of schooling for population over 25 are from Barro and Lee (1994). An industry's external financing dependence (capital expenditures minus cash flow from operations, scaled by capex) is computed from U.S. Compustat firms in the 1980s (and 1970s for robustness). Accounting standards (CIFAR) and legal origin variables (La Porta et al.) are also used.
institutional_context: The setting is the cross-country variation in the development of domestic financial systems at the start of the 1980s, combined with persistent technological differences in industries' reliance on outside funds. Countries differ markedly in the size and sophistication of their banking and equity markets due in part to historical and legal accidents — for instance, common-law former British colonies (e.g., Malaysia, Singapore) tended to develop deeper equity markets, while civil-law countries (e.g., Belgium) had smaller stock markets. International capital markets are imperfectly integrated (home bias, savings-investment correlations), so firms rely largely on domestic finance. Within any country, some manufacturing industries (e.g., pharmaceuticals, computers, electrical machinery) inherently require substantial outside funds because of long gestation periods, large initial scale, or limited internal cash generation, while others (e.g., tobacco, leather) generate cash in excess of investment needs. This combination creates differential exposure of industries to local financial conditions during the 1980-1990 decade.

_legacy_v1_ground_truth.identification_strategy: IV — treatment = financial development, control = less financially dependent industries; instrument = initial financial development level

key_variables.treatment: financial development level in a country

_legacy_v1_ground_truth.conclusion_detail: Financial development positively impacts the growth of industries that are more dependent on external finance.
_legacy_v1_ground_truth.main_effect: Industries more dependent on external finance grow faster in countries with more developed financial markets.
